h1: Malt whisky from a brewery wash
title: Malt Whisky From a Brewery Wash | Craft Beer School
desc: How a whisky wash differs from brewery wort and what a brewer must change about boiling, hops, gravity and yeast to make malt whisky.
teaser: A brewery can make a whisky wash. But it has to stop doing some of the things that make it good at beer.
standfirst: Brewers already mash malt and ferment wort, so making a wash for malt whisky looks easy. The basics are close. The differences, no boil and no hops chief among them, change the spirit yield and the flavour a lot.
sections: A wash is unhopped, unboiled beer

In whisky terms, the wash is the fermented liquid that goes into the wash still. It is close to a strong, cloudy, unhopped beer of around 8% ABV. The mashing is familiar to any brewer: milled malt and hot water, a conversion rest, then run-off. After that the processes split.

Distillers do not boil the wort. They do not add hops. They ferment fast and dry with distilling yeast. Each of these changes has a reason. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky covers where malt whisky sits.
No boil keeps the enzymes working

A brewer boils wort for about an hour. That sterilises it, drives off unwanted compounds, sets the hops and destroys the malt enzymes, so the dextrins that give beer body stay in the glass.

A distiller wants the opposite. Unboiled wort still carries active enzymes into the washback, where they keep breaking dextrins into fermentable sugar while the yeast works. The wash ferments much drier, often to a gravity below 1.000. It yields more alcohol per tonne of malt. A brewery wort that has been boiled will finish with more residual extract and give fewer litres of spirit.
Hops do not belong in the still

Hops add bitterness and aroma to beer. In a wash they add nothing useful for most malt whisky styles and can cause trouble. Hop compounds can carry through distillation as grassy, vegetal or resinous notes. Hopped wash may foam more in the still. If you want a hopped spirit, that is a different product with its own rules.

The practical rule for a brewery making wash is simple: separate the wash production from hop handling. That includes the kettle, the whirlpool and any line that carries hopped wort.

Washes are typically fermented from an original gravity around 1.050 to 1.060, though distilleries vary. Distilling yeast strains tolerate higher alcohol and ferment quickly. Fermentations often run two to four days. Longer fermentations are associated with fruitier, more complex new make, partly from bacterial activity late in the ferment.

Brewer's ale yeast can be used and is sometimes chosen deliberately for ester character, but it may finish less dry. Measure attenuation and alcohol in the wash for each yeast and record the spirit yield that follows.
Clear or cloudy wort changes the spirit

Brewers work hard for clear wort. Distillers argue about it. Clear wort is commonly associated with a lighter, fruitier new make. Cloudy wort, carrying more grain solids into the washback, tends to give heavier, nuttier or more cereal notes. Both are legitimate. Choose on purpose.

The floor detail we would insist on: watch the washback temperature. Without the cooling capacity a brewery uses for lager, a vigorous distilling ferment in Indian heat can climb past the low thirties in °C, stress the yeast and produce harsh flavours that carry into the spirit. Plan cooling before you plan volume.

For malt whisky, the mash should be malted barley only. Many Indian breweries use rice or maize adjuncts in their beer. Those have no place in a wash meant for malt whisky. Keep separate grist records for every wash.

Under the Scotch definition, mashing must happen at the distillery itself, so a wash bought in from a separate brewery would not qualify there. Indian standards and state rules differ, so check the current notification. If export is in the plan, design to the strict version. Our guide to Indian single malt covers the category.

A brewery licence does not allow distillation. Moving wash from a brewery to a distillery is usually a controlled movement between licensed premises. Rules vary by state and change, so check the current notification or work with a licensing adviser before you plan any wash supply arrangement.

Brewing knowledge transfers well into distilling. But the changes above decide whether the spirit is good and whether it is legal. A distilling course closes that gap for brewers who already know their way around a mash tun. Our guide to Indian six-row barley covers the raw material.

Your first step: brew one small batch of all-malt wort, skip the boil and hops, ferment it with a distilling yeast and record the final gravity against your usual beer.
faqs: Can a brewery make wash for whisky?
The process is similar, but the wash should be unboiled, unhopped and all malt. Distillation itself needs a separate licence. Rules vary by state.
Why do distillers not boil the wort?
Leaving the wort unboiled keeps malt enzymes active, so they convert more dextrins into sugar during fermentation. The wash ferments drier and yields more alcohol.
What strength is a whisky wash?
Typically around 8% ABV, fermented from an original gravity of roughly 1.050 to 1.060 down to below 1.000.
Can hopped beer be distilled into whisky?
It can be distilled, but hop compounds carry into the spirit and can cause foaming. Most malt whisky is made from unhopped wash.
